# Exact hinge compression when every integer fiber is exposed

This is a conditional cap-cover compression theorem. It preserves an
already available cap budget and does not supply a low-budget cover of
a general mixed-integer convex body. The hypothesis that every base
point is a vertex is substantive.

Let `d>=1`, let P be a finite nonempty subset of `R^n`, and let each
`K_z subset R^d`, `z in P`, be a full-dimensional compact convex body.
Assume every point of P is a vertex of `conv(P)`. Write

    S=union_z ({z} x K_z),
    mu=sum_z vol_d,  M=mu(S),
    D=conv union_z(K_z-K_z).

The body D is centrally symmetric and full dimensional. For a cap
represented by `L(z,x)=a dot z+u dot x-b`, with `u!=0`, set

    Psi_D(L)=integral_S (L)_+ dmu / h_D(u).

All caps in this note are closed, and coverage means coverage of every
point of every fiber, including its boundary.

## 1. The compression theorem

Suppose a finite family of nonvertical caps `{L_i>=0}` covers S and
each has mass at most `tau M`. Then there is another cover with at most
`|P|(d+1)` nonvertical caps such that:

1. Every new cap meets exactly one integer fiber in positive measure
   and is strictly disjoint from every other integer fiber.
2. Every new cap has positive mass strictly smaller than its own fiber
   volume and has mass at most `tau M`.
3. The sum of the new D-normalized hinges is no larger than the sum
   for the original cover.
4. The new sum is at most

       min{(d+1)M, |P|(d+1) tau M}.

If additionally `P=conv(P) intersect Z^n`, then `|P|<=2^n`, so the new
cover uses at most the full mixed Helly count `N0=2^n(d+1)` and its
hinge is at most `min{d+1,N0 tau}M`.

### Proof of the fiberwise extraction

Fix z. The restrictions of the original caps cover K_z. A subfamily of
at most d+1 restrictions still covers K_z. Here is a direct finite
proof retaining closed boundaries. Let x_* minimize the continuous
convex function `f(x)=max_i L_i(z,x)` on K_z. Coverage says its minimum
is nonnegative. The finite minimax separation for affine functions on
a compact convex set supplies nonnegative weights lambda on indices
active at x_*, summing to one, such that

    U=sum_i lambda_i u_i,
    U dot (x-x_*)>=0 for every x in K_z.

Equivalently, the weighted affine function is minimized at x_* over
K_z. This is the full-fiber minimax certificate proved in Section 3 of
`candidate de8d1a3251731edd`. Apply finite
Caratheodory reduction to U in the convex hull of the active u_i's:
if more than d+1 weights are positive, an affine dependence permits
moving them until one weight vanishes without changing their sum or
U; repeat. Every retained index is still active at x_*. Therefore

    sum_i lambda_i L_i(z,x)
       =f(x_*)+U dot (x-x_*)>=0

for every x in K_z. At least one retained cap contains x, proving the
closed cover by at most d+1 caps.

If one of these caps contains all of K_z, use only that cap for the
next step. Otherwise remove all zero-volume caps. This removal still
leaves a cover: zero-volume affine caps have no points in the interior
of K_z, and the union of the remaining finitely many closed caps
contains that interior, hence its closure K_z. The remaining caps have
mass strictly between zero and the fiber volume.

### Replacing a whole-fiber cap without increasing hinge

Suppose the selected cap contains all of K_z and has continuous normal
u. Put `X=u dot x`, let m be the median of X under uniform volume on
K_z, and replace the cap on this fiber by

    X-m>=0,   m-X>=0.

Because K_z is full dimensional and u is nonzero, its scalar
projection is atomless and has strictly positive mass on every
nonempty interior interval. Thus m is interior to the projection and
the two closed caps each have exactly half the fiber volume. They
cover K_z and each has mass no larger than the original whole-fiber
cap.

If the original threshold on the fiber is t, then
`t<=min_(K_z) X`. The new unnormalized hinge sum is
`integral |X-m|`. A median minimizes `integral |X-s|` over real s:
the one-sided slopes are the mass below s minus the mass above s,
with the interval between those values at an atom; here there are no
atoms. Consequently

    integral |X-m| <= integral |X-t|
                      = integral (X-t)_+.

The denominator is unchanged because `h_D(-u)=h_D(u)`. The new two
caps therefore cost no more than that original cap. Their number is
at most d+1, including in dimension one.

### Exact ambient isolation

For each vertex z choose an affine base function q_z with

    q_z(z)=0,   q_z(w)>0 for every other w in P.

Such a function exists because z is an exposed vertex of a finite
polytope. A chosen local margin `u dot x-t` extends to the ambient
margin

    u dot x-t-A q_z(w).

At its own base point it is unchanged. Since every other K_w is
compact and there are only finitely many of them, a finite sufficiently
large A makes this margin strictly negative on every other fiber.
Thus the new ambient cap has exactly its local mass and local hinge.
Its continuous normal remains u, so its normalization is unchanged.
Each new cap mass is at most that of an original cap selected at this
fiber; it therefore obeys the original individual budget `tau M`.

For each z, extraction only removes terms from the original local
hinge sum, and the possible median replacement does not increase it.
Summing these inequalities over fibers proves the global hinge
inequality. There is no double counting: an original cap chosen in
several fibers contributes only its distinct original local integrals.

Every resulting local cap cuts its body properly. Its positive margin
is therefore bounded above on K_z by

    max_(K_z) u dot x-min_(K_z) u dot x
       =h_(K_z-K_z)(u)<=h_D(u).

Its normalized hinge is at most its cap mass. There are at most d+1
caps per fiber, whose masses are each at most the fiber volume and
at most tau M. This proves both displayed upper bounds.

Finally, for lattice-convex P in convex position, two distinct points
of the same parity would have an integer midpoint in conv(P), hence
in P. That midpoint would not be a vertex, a contradiction. Thus P
has at most one point of each of the 2^n parity classes. This is the
only use of the integer structure in the compression proof. QED.

## 2. Exact optimum for interval fibers

Under the same exposed-base hypothesis, now take d=1 and let the
fiber lengths be w_z>0. Put `W=max_z w_z`, so `D=[-W,W]`.
If any finite nonvertical cap cover with budget tau M exists, then

    tau M>=W/2.                                            (1)

Indeed a cap covering the midpoint of a longest interval has at least
half that interval's length in its own fiber, regardless of its
integer tilt or of the other fibers. Isolated midpoint pairs therefore
give a budget-feasible cover using exactly 2|P| caps.

The exact minimum over ALL finite covers, and hence over covers with
at most `2|P|`, is

    Psi_min=(1/(4W)) sum_z w_z^2.                         (2)

To prove the lower bound, normalize every continuous normal to +1 or
-1. On a single interval [l,r] of length w, only the least threshold
among upper caps and the greatest threshold among lower caps matter
for coverage. Keeping those two terms can only lower the hinge sum.
If only one orientation is present, a cap of that orientation must
contain the whole interval, giving hinge at least w^2/2.

If both orientations are present, write their thresholds t and s,
so the margins are x-t and s-x. If either cap contains the whole
interval, the same w^2/2 lower bound applies. Otherwise a cover requires
`l<=t<=s<=r`. Their hinge sum is

    ((r-t)^2+(s-l)^2)/2
       >=((r-t)^2+(t-l)^2)/2>=w^2/4.

The last minimum occurs at `t=s=(l+r)/2`. Dividing by W and summing
over fibers proves (2). Isolating each midpoint pair gives equality,
and (1) proves its budget feasibility. Thus neither nonaffine vertical
heights nor unequal interval volumes produce an obstruction in this
exposed-base, full-cardinality regime.

The formulas also show that an arbitrary input cover is replaced by
an exact globally minimizing cover, not merely by one whose hinge
has some unspecified finite bound.

## 3. The unresolved restriction

For a nonvertex p in P, no affine q_p can vanish at p and be strictly
positive at all other indices: any convex representation of p would
contradict that strict inequality. The ambient isolation step therefore
fails exactly at nonextreme indices. The proof does not preserve the
budget if it is replaced by a cap on the convex hull of several
fibers, because that can add cap mass at other integer indices.

Consequently this theorem settles a conditional compression problem on
every convex-position integer support, for arbitrary continuous
dimension, shapes, heights, volumes, and input cap count. It does not
establish the desired compression for a general lattice-convex support
with nonextreme points, and it supplies no affirmative proof of OC.
